days.title: Aerobic vs Anaerobic Respiration
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate aerobic from anaerobic respiration.
  • Explain the role of oxygen.
  • Describe fermentation types.
  • Compare ATP yield.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Aerobic respiration — requires oxygen; produces ~36–38 ATP per glucose.
  • Anaerobic respiration — no oxygen; produces 2 ATP per glucose.
  • Fermentation — anaerobic pathway that regenerates NAD⁺.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Aerobic vs Anaerobic

FeatureAerobicAnaerobic
OxygenRequiredNot required
ATP yield~36–382
LocationCytoplasm + mitochondriaCytoplasm
ProductsCO₂ + H₂OLactic acid or ethanol + CO₂

B. Types of Fermentation

  • Lactic acid fermentation — muscle cells (produces lactate)
  • Alcoholic fermentation — yeast (produces ethanol + CO₂)

💬 Let's Discuss

Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose; cellular respiration releases it as ATP. Every living cell — plant, animal, fungus or bacterium — must do some form of respiration. The big question is: is oxygen available?

Aerobic respiration uses oxygen and breaks glucose completely into CO₂ and H₂O: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + about 36–38 ATP. It has four stages: glycolysis (cytoplasm), pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle (mitochondrial matrix), and the electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane). Notice the equation is the reverse of photosynthesis.

Anaerobic pathways work without oxygen. Glycolysis can still run, but it quickly uses up NAD⁺. Fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can keep going, yielding only 2 ATP per glucose — about 18 times less. In lactic acid fermentation, pyruvate becomes lactate; your muscle cells do this during a hard sprint when oxygen cannot be delivered fast enough, and lactobacilli use it to make yogurt and burong mangga. In alcoholic fermentation, yeast turns pyruvate into ethanol and CO₂; the CO₂ makes pandesal dough rise and the ethanol is used in making tuba and basi.

Why is aerobic respiration so much better? Because oxygen is a powerful electron acceptor that lets the ETC run, pulling far more energy out of each glucose. That is why organisms with high energy needs, like birds and mammals, depend on oxygen.

Common mistake: believing plants do photosynthesis instead of respiration. Plants respire all the time, day and night; in daylight, photosynthesis simply outpaces it.

days.title: Glycolysis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the overall process of cellular respiration.
  • Explain the steps of glycolysis.
  • Identify the products of glycolysis.
  • Explain substrate-level phosphorylation.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Glycolysis — breakdown of glucose into 2 pyruvate.
  • Substrate-level phosphorylation — direct ATP production.
  • Net ATP — 2 ATP per glucose (4 produced − 2 used).
  • NADH — carries electrons to the ETC.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Glycolysis Overview

Occurs in cytoplasm. Glucose (6C) is split into 2 pyruvate (3C) molecules.

B. Two Phases

  • Investment phase — 2 ATP used to activate glucose
  • Payoff phase — 4 ATP and 2 NADH produced

C. Net Products (per glucose)

  • 2 ATP (net)
  • 2 NADH
  • 2 pyruvate

💬 Let's Discuss

Glycolysis ("sugar splitting") is the first stage of both aerobic respiration and fermentation, and it happens in the cytoplasm without needing oxygen. It is probably the oldest energy pathway — found in almost every organism — which suggests it evolved before Earth's air had much oxygen.

In about ten enzyme-controlled steps, one six-carbon glucose is split into two three-carbon pyruvate molecules. The steps fall into two phases. In the energy-investment phase, the cell spends 2 ATP to add phosphates to glucose. This sounds wasteful, but it is like spending money on a jeepney fare to get to work: it "activates" the molecule and traps it inside the cell. In the energy-payoff phase, the molecule is split and oxidized, producing 4 ATP and 2 NADH.

Net result per glucose: 2 pyruvate, 2 ATP (4 made − 2 spent), and 2 NADH. The ATP here is made by substrate-level phosphorylation — an enzyme moves a phosphate directly from a substrate to ADP.

What happens next depends on oxygen. With oxygen, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion and NADH sends its electrons to the ETC to make more ATP. Without oxygen, pyruvate is converted to lactate or ethanol to recycle NADH back to NAD⁺. Cancer cells and red blood cells (which have no mitochondria) rely heavily on glycolysis.

Common mistake: saying glycolysis produces 4 ATP. It makes 4, but the net gain is 2 because 2 were invested.

pairs.why: Glycolysis splits one glucose into two pyruvate.
Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm.
The investment phase spends 2 ATP to activate glucose.
The payoff phase makes 4 ATP.
4 made − 2 spent = net 2 ATP.
NADH carries high-energy electrons to the ETC.

days.title: Krebs Cycle
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the Krebs cycle.
  • Trace the fate of pyruvate.
  • Identify the products of the Krebs cycle.
  • Explain the role of the Krebs cycle in metabolism.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Pyruvate oxidation — pyruvate → acetyl-CoA.
  • Krebs cycle — also called the citric acid cycle or TCA cycle.
  • Location — mitochondrial matrix.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Pyruvate Oxidation

Each pyruvate (3C) loses CO₂ and becomes acetyl-CoA (2C). Produces 1 NADH per pyruvate.

B. Krebs Cycle (per acetyl-CoA)

ProductCount
CO₂2
NADH3
FADH₂1
ATP1

C. Per Glucose (2 turns)

  • 6 NADH
  • 2 FADH₂
  • 2 ATP
  • 4 CO₂

💬 Let's Discuss

When oxygen is present, the two pyruvates from glycolysis enter the mitochondrion. First comes pyruvate oxidation (the link reaction): each three-carbon pyruvate loses one carbon as CO₂, is oxidized (making NADH), and joins coenzyme A to form two-carbon acetyl-CoA. This is the "ticket" into the Krebs cycle.

The Krebs cycle (also called the citric acid cycle, after its first product) happens in the mitochondrial matrix. Acetyl-CoA combines with a four-carbon molecule (oxaloacetate) to form six-carbon citrate. Through a series of steps, citrate is gradually oxidized: two carbons leave as 2 CO₂, and the four-carbon starting molecule is regenerated, so the cycle can turn again.

Each turn produces 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂ and 1 ATP (by substrate-level phosphorylation). Since one glucose gives two pyruvates, the cycle turns twice per glucose, giving 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂ and 2 ATP. By the end of the Krebs cycle, all six carbons of the original glucose have been released as CO₂ — this is the CO₂ you breathe out.

Notice how little ATP the cycle makes directly. Its real product is loaded electron carriers (NADH and FADH₂). Like charged batteries, they carry high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain, where most of the ATP will be made.

Common mistake: thinking the Krebs cycle uses oxygen directly. It does not, but it stops without oxygen, because the ETC cannot unload NADH and FADH₂ back into NAD⁺ and FAD.

days.title: Electron Transport Chain & Chemiosmosis
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the electron transport chain.
  • Explain chemiosmosis.
  • Explain the role of oxygen.
  • Summarize the ATP yield of respiration.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Electron transport chain (ETC) — series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
  • Chemiosmosis — ATP production via H⁺ gradient.
  • ATP synthase — enzyme that produces ATP.
  • Oxygen — final electron acceptor; forms water.

📚 Lesson Content

A. The ETC

NADH and FADH₂ drop electrons at protein complexes. Electrons move through the chain, releasing energy that pumps H⁺ into the intermembrane space.

B. Chemiosmosis

H⁺ flows back through ATP synthase into the matrix, driving ATP production (~26–28 ATP).

C. Oxygen's Role

O₂ is the final electron acceptor. It combines with electrons and H⁺ to form H₂O. Without O₂, the ETC backs up.

D. Total ATP Yield (Aerobic)

  • Glycolysis: 2 ATP
  • Krebs: 2 ATP
  • ETC: ~32–34 ATP
  • Total: ~36–38 ATP

💬 Let's Discuss

The final stage makes most of the ATP. The electron transport chain (ETC) is a series of protein complexes in the inner mitochondrial membrane — the same membrane folded into cristae to give more room for these proteins.

NADH and FADH₂ from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle drop off their high-energy electrons at the chain. The electrons pass from one complex to the next, each step releasing a small amount of energy. The complexes use that energy to pump H⁺ ions from the matrix into the intermembrane space, building up a high concentration there — like water stored behind a dam.

At the end of the chain, the electrons need somewhere to go. Oxygen is the final electron acceptor: it combines with electrons and H⁺ to form water. That is the only reason we need to breathe oxygen.

Meanwhile, H⁺ ions rush back into the matrix through ATP synthase, a molecular turbine that spins and joins ADP with phosphate. This process, chemiosmosis, together with the ETC is called oxidative phosphorylation, and it produces about 32–34 ATP per glucose — around 90% of the total of ~36–38 ATP.

Without oxygen, electrons pile up, the chain stops, NADH cannot be recycled, and the Krebs cycle halts too. The cell must fall back on fermentation. Cyanide is deadly because it blocks the last complex of the ETC, stopping ATP production almost instantly.

Common mistake: saying the ETC makes ATP directly. The ETC builds the H⁺ gradient; ATP synthase makes the ATP.

pairs.why: The ETC is a chain of electron carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
Chemiosmosis uses an H⁺ gradient to make ATP.
ATP synthase turns H⁺ flow into ATP.

Aerobic respiration totals about 36–38 ATP per glucose.
